cover_design.label: TAGALOG
cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Tagalog for complete beginners — from saying hello in Manila to telling the story of last weekend.

product.title: Tagalog 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Tagalog: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Tagalog builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with a stress-marked, English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Tagalog is spelled the way it's spoken and borrows freely from Spanish and English, so words come quickly. Each unit tackles the three things that really set it apart: the markers ang/ng/sa, verb focus, and the little particles that set the tone of every sentence.

blocks.text: Tagalog has a reputation for being exotic, and in one way it is: almost nothing in it works like English. But it hands beginners a few gifts right away. *Anak* is "child". *Mata* is "eye". *Lima* is "five". *Mahal* means "expensive" — and also "dear, beloved". Short, regular words, spelled exactly as they sound.

Tagalog belongs to the Austronesian family, the same family as Malay and Indonesian, Hawaiian and Māori. If you know any Malay or Indonesian, you'll spot hundreds of shared words. If you know some Spanish, you'll spot hundreds more: the Philippines was a Spanish colony for over three centuries. And English, the country's second official language, is everywhere.

The real challenge lies elsewhere: **in how sentences are put together**. English marks who did what by word order. Tagalog marks it with three little words — *ang*, *ng* and *sa* — and with the shape of the verb itself. *Kumain ang bata ng mangga* and *Kinain ng bata ang mangga* use exactly the same words, but the spotlight falls in a different place.

That is where all the difficulty of this language lies, and this course doesn't put it off. The marker *ang* arrives in unit 2, all three markers are in place by unit 5, and verb focus gets three units in a row to itself (units 10, 11, 12) — not one paragraph in the last chapter.

The second thing to know from the start: **Tagalog verbs don't mark time, they mark stages.** There is no "past" and "future" as in English. Instead: completed, in progress, not yet begun. Once you get used to it, it is a surprisingly natural way to see events.

The third, and the fastest way to sound like a local: **little particles**. *Na*, *pa*, *po*, *ba*, *lang*, *naman*, *daw*, *kasi*. These one-syllable words carry politeness, surprise and warmth. A foreigner with perfect grammar who never uses them sounds like a walking phrasebook.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20-30 undisturbed minutes, not two hours in bits and pieces. Language sticks through short, frequent repetition, not one long assault.

Read aloud. Tagalog spelling is honest — almost every letter is read as written — but **word stress** isn't written, and the wrong stress can change the meaning (*báka* cow, *bakâ* maybe). The "Say it" column in this course marks the stressed syllable in CAPITALS.

Don't expect Tagalog sentences to work like English ones. Shared words are a gift; the grammar is where the real work is. Even familiar-looking words can surprise you: *mahal* is both "expensive" and "beloved", and *masarap* is used for food, sleep and weather alike.
Use *po* from day one. In the Philippines that one word separates the polite from the rude, and it costs you a single syllable.

blocks.text: The explanations are deliberately short. What's long isn't the theory, it's the practice.
Enjoy the journey. *Good luck at mabuhay!*

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be done in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same structure, in a deliberate order:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Tagalog aloud without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the translation. It's the part people skip most, yet it's where you see how Tagalog *thinks*. For example, *Ako si Budi* literally means "I (am) si Budi", and *Masarap ang adobo* means "tasty the adobo" — the description comes first, the thing comes after.
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the unit's new words, with a pronunciation guide. The stressed syllable is in CAPITALS, and a ' at the end marks a catch in the throat (a glottal stop).
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Tagalog, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Tagalog sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: Tagalog or Filipino?
items: *Tagalog* is the native language of Manila and the surrounding region. *Filipino* is the national language of the Philippines, built on Tagalog plus loanwords from other Philippine languages and from English.

For a beginner the difference is barely noticeable: what you learn here is the language people use on the street, at the market and on Philippine TV. That's why this course is called Tagalog, but everything in it is perfectly good Filipino.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Tagalog spelling is honest, but its honesty stops at word stress — and stress is the one thing in this language that can really make you say something you didn't mean.

Before unit 1, it's worth seeing how much you're starting with. Tagalog shares a deep layer of everyday words with its Austronesian relatives (fun fact: many are nearly identical in Malay and Indonesian), a big layer from Spanish, and a growing layer from English.

blocks.text: The Spanish legacy — 333 years
The Philippines was ruled by Spain for more than three centuries, and Tagalog kept thousands of Spanish words. If you know a little Spanish, you've already got a head start:

Then there's English, which in the Philippines isn't a foreign language but the second official one. People in Manila mix the two freely — *Taglish* — so a sentence like *Nag-shopping ako kahapon* (I went shopping yesterday) sounds perfectly normal. This course teaches the Tagalog form first, then tells you where real people actually use the English word.

blocks.title: Why this matters
items: Words will come; you'll pick them up faster than you expect. The real work is learning to **put them together** — the three markers *ang/ng/sa*, verb focus, and the particles.
That's why this course gives a big share to grammar and a small share to word lists. Vocabulary will come by itself; sentence structure won't.

blocks.text: The good news fits in one sentence: **Tagalog is written the way it's spoken.** Five pure vowels, mostly familiar consonants, no silent letters and no spelling surprises.
What's left are four things, and all four are explained on these pages. The "Say it" guide in this course uses English-style spelling: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo.
1. Five vowels — but there used to be three

head: Letter
Sound
Example
Meaning
rows: *oh*, a pure o (no *w* at the end)

blocks.text: Before the Spanish arrived, Tagalog had only **three** vowels: *a*, *i* and *u*. The letters *e* and *o* came later through loanwords. That history still shows: *i* and *e* often swap, and so do *u* and *o*. Two vowel combinations are worth knowing too: *ay* sounds like *eye* (written *ai* in our guide) and *aw* like *how* (written *ow*).

items: *babae* (woman) is often heard as *babai*
*lalaki* (man) is also written *lalake*
*noon* and *nuon*, *ito* and *itu* — the same swap
The practical rule: **u inside the word, o at the end**. *Buhok* (hair), not *bohok*; *utos* (order), not *otos*.

blocks.text: 2. Ng — one letter, not two

In the Tagalog alphabet (*abakada*), **ng** counts as **one letter**, with its own place between N and O. It sounds exactly like the "ng" in *singer* — nothing new there. What's new is **where it can stand**.

head: Word
Say it
Meaning
Note
rows: ng at the **start** of a word — impossible in English
ng in the middle, as in *hanger*
ng at the end, as in *sing*

blocks.title: Two words you must know how to say
items: **ng** (a marker that appears on every page of this course) is pronounced **nahng** — not "eng", not just "ng". The spelling is short because of an old printing tradition; the sound is full.
**mga** (the plural marker) is pronounced **mah-NGAH**. It's a fossilized abbreviation; not a single letter is read as written.

blocks.text: 3. Stress (diin) — the one thing that can change your meaning

Everyday Tagalog spelling **doesn't show stress**. Dictionaries and textbooks use accent marks (*á*, *à*, *â*), but newspapers, signs and text messages don't. So you have to learn the stress together with the word, just as you learn its sounds.
Throughout this course, the **Say it** column writes the stressed syllable in CAPITALS. Treat it as part of the word, not as decoration.
4. The glottal stop (impit)

You already have this sound without knowing it: it's the catch in the throat in the middle of *uh-oh*, or in the way many speakers say *bu'on* for "button". In Tagalog, that catch can change the meaning.

head: Word
Say it
Meaning
rows: small child (with a catch at the end)

blocks.text: In this course the glottal stop is marked with **'** in the Say it column. If you leave it out, you'll still be understood — but you'll sound foreign. If you get the stress wrong, sometimes you won't be understood at all.
Letters that aren't native to Tagalog

The original *abakada* had only 20 letters: *a b k d e g h i l m n ng o p r s t u w y*. The letters **c, f, j, ñ, q, v, x, z** came in through Spanish and English, and are used only in names and loanwords that haven't been localized. That's why many loanwords are respelled the way they sound:

Notice the recurring pattern: **v becomes b**, **f becomes p**, **c becomes k**, **j becomes h**. The same pattern runs in Tagalog speakers' heads when they pronounce English words — and knowing it makes your ear much quicker at catching Taglish.
d that turns into r
One last sound rule you'll meet often: **d between two vowels becomes r**. This isn't an exception, it's a living habit.

items: *dami* (amount) → *marami* (many, a lot) — not *madami*
*dating* (arrive) → *dumarating* (is arriving)
*doon* (there) → *naroon* (is there)
*din* (too) → *rin* after a word ending in a vowel: *ako rin*, but *ikaw din*

blocks.title: In short
items: Read every letter as written, with pure vowels: ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. That's 90% of the job.
Remember **ng = nahng** and **mga = mah-NGAH**.
Learn stress together with the word — CAPITALS in the Say it column.
The glottal stop (the ' mark) makes you sound local; stress makes you understood.

head: Common nouns
Personal names (one)

rows: Doer or thing not in the spotlight

blocks.text: Plural of common nouns: add *mga* after the marker — *ang mga bata*, *ng mga bata*, *sa mga bata*.
Personal pronouns — three sets
*Ikaw* stands at the front of a sentence, *ka* attaches after the first word: *Ikaw ba ang guro?* but *Guro ka ba?*
Demonstratives
Verb aspect — not time, but stages

The pattern behind it all: **the first syllable is repeated** for "ongoing" and "upcoming"; **the infix -in-** (or the prefix *na-*/*nag-*) marks "already begun". Completed and ongoing have both begun; not-begun and upcoming both haven't.
Verb focus — the spotlight

head: Focus
Affix
Example
Literal meaning
rows: the-thing-eaten by the child: the mango

blocks.text: One rule explains it all: **whatever is marked with *ang* is in the spotlight, and the verb's form must match that spotlight.** English does something similar with active and passive ("the child ate the mango" / "the mango was eaten"), but Tagalog has four spotlights, not two — and none of them feels "passive".
Sentences without a verb
Notice: the description stands **in front**, the thing follows. It's the reverse of English, and the single biggest habit change you'll need to practice.
Negation

head: What's negated
Word
Example
rows: Hindi ako guro. / Hindi siya kumain.
Wala akong pera. / Wala si Ana.

blocks.text: Order of enclitic particles
Particles always attach **after the first word** of the sentence, and their order among themselves is fixed: one-syllable ones come first.

items: One syllable: *na*, *pa*, *ba*, *po*, *ka*, *mo*, *ko*, *rin/din*, *daw/raw*, *pala*, *lang*
Usual order: **ka/ko/mo + na/pa + po + ba + rin + daw/pala/naman**
Stacked example: *Kumain ka na ba?* (Have you eaten?) — *Hindi pa po ako kumakain.* (I haven't eaten yet, sir/ma'am.)

blocks.text: The linker na / -ng

head: First word ends in
Form
Example
rows: gutom → gutom na; sarap → masarap**na**; *kanin* → kani**ng** mainit

blocks.text: The linker is used whenever two words describe each other: adjective + noun, number + noun, *gusto* + verb, and relative clauses. It has no meaning of its own — it just glues.
These thirty verbs cover most of everyday conversation. The **Completed / Ongoing / Upcoming** columns use actor focus, the form you'll say most often.

blocks.title: How to use this table
items: Don't memorize it as a table. Take five rows a day, make one sentence for each column, and say them out loud.

Notice that **the "not begun" and "completed" forms are identical** for -UM- verbs. Only their place in the sentence tells them apart: after *gusto*, *dapat* or *huwag*, the action hasn't happened yet.

blocks.text: If you've reached this page after really working through all twenty units, your level is roughly **a full A1, heading for A2**: you can introduce yourself, shop, order food, ask for directions, talk about yesterday, and share your plans. What you don't have yet is speed — and no book can give you that.
Three things that raise your level fastest

items: **Listen to Philippine news.** GMA and ABS-CBN use clear standard Tagalog, and the news repeats the same vocabulary every day — near-ideal learning conditions.
**Watch teleserye (TV dramas) with English subtitles.** This is where you hear the particles at work: *naman*, *kasi*, *pala*, *ha* — things that never fully show up in a textbook.

**Talk to people.** Filipinos are among the friendliest people anywhere toward learners of their language, because they rarely meet foreigners who bother to learn Tagalog. *Nag-aaral po ako ng Tagalog* almost always earns a smile.

blocks.title: One last piece of advice
items: Tagalog gives you a big head start at the beginning (short, regular words) and a big bill in the middle (verb focus). Many people quit right at units 10-12, where that bill falls due.
If you've made it here, the hardest part is behind you. The rest is repetition — and repetition isn't hard, it just takes time.
*Kaya mo 'yan!* — You can do it.
